input_signals.name: Accruals While Leverage Is Rising
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Distress is a trajectory, not just a level: soft accrual-based earnings reported in the same year that the liability-to-asset ratio is climbing indicate a firm funding working-capital expansion with new debt, and it is this dynamic combination — not static leverage — that precedes forced reversal and write-downs.
input_signals.reasoning: Conditioning on the change in leverage rather than its level tests a deterioration mechanism that is only weakly correlated with the static leverage rank used elsewhere in the archive, so it teaches a distinguishable lesson about which distress state matters. Stable high-leverage utilities and REITs, which contaminate level-based conditioning, receive no weight here unless their balance sheets are actually worsening.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( add( sub( wcap, che ), dlc ), 1 ), dp ), at ), 1 ) ), rank( delta( ratio( lt, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Accruals Against Rollover Pressure
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What makes accruals dangerous is near-term cash need rather than total indebtedness: a firm whose debt is concentrated in current maturities must convert receivables and inventory into cash within months, so accrual-heavy earnings at such firms are the least likely to survive contact with the refinancing calendar.
input_signals.reasoning: The short-term share of total debt is close to orthogonal to the leverage level, so pairing it with the same centered accrual leg as signal 1 isolates exactly which dimension of distress amplifies accrual mispricing — a maturity-structure lesson the archive has not yet tested. It also matches the economic story's emphasis on liquidity pressure rather than solvency.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( add( sub( wcap, che ), dlc ), 1 ), dp ), at ), 1 ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt Financed Accrual Build
input_signals.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dlc, dltt), 1), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The dangerous case is not accruals as such but accruals that had to be funded externally: a firm whose receivables and inventory swell while it simultaneously raises new short- and long-term debt is converting borrowed cash into soft assets, and that combination precedes both accrual reversal and rising default risk.
input_signals.reasoning: MIN of two demeaned legs is a conjunction, not a monotone reweighting of the accrual leg, so a firm with large accruals but no new borrowing (or large borrowing but no accrual build) is not flagged — this is exactly what the published Sloan sort cannot express and it is what the critic asked for. The short leg is symmetric and economically clean: firms generating cash while retiring debt, which is the survivorship profile the accrual-distress story predicts should outperform.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( add( sub( wcap, che ), dlc ), 1 ), dp ), at ), 1 ) ), zscore( winsor( ratio( delta( add( dlc, dltt ), 1 ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Accrual Spike Against Own History In Fragile Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 5)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: An accrual that is extreme relative to the firm's own five-year history is a far stronger manipulation flag than an accrual that is merely large in the cross-section, because it controls for the firm's stable business model; such a self-referential spike should be most reversal-prone at firms with high leverage and accumulated deficits.
input_signals.reasoning: This restores the mispricing sign rather than fitting the single generation-1 alpha, so it is an independent test rather than reverse-engineering, while still exploiting time-series information about accrual behavior. TS_RANK measures position in the firm's own distribution instead of volatility, which sidesteps the contested accrual-quality risk premium and produces a bounded, outlier-resistant accrual leg that is demeaned before the distress rank modulates its slope.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( ts_rank( ratio( sub( delta( add( sub( wcap, che ), dlc ), 1 ), dp ), at ), 5 ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Accrual Build Per Dollar Of Equity Cushion
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), MAX(ceq, che)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically relevant scale for an accrual is the loss-absorbing capital that must absorb its reversal, not total assets: the same dollar of soft working-capital growth is trivial for a firm with a thick book equity cushion and existential for a thinly capitalized one, so deflating by the cushion embeds distress directly in the measurement.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the cosmetic industry-neutral variant with a genuinely different functional form — distress enters as a deflator that is decreasing in fragility, which is the direction the generation-0 liability-deflator error got backwards — allowing us to learn whether cushion-scaling dominates multiplicative conditioning. Flooring the denominator at cash keeps it positive for near-zero or negative book equity firms, and 1% winsorization controls the thin-cushion tail while retaining the broad coverage of balance-sheet inputs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( delta( add( sub( wcap, che ), dlc ), 1 ), dp ), max( ceq, che ) ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Accruals Against Cash Adjusted Rollover Pressure
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Rollover pressure only bites when the firm cannot self-fund the maturing claim, so the conditioning state should combine a short-maturity debt structure with a thin cash buffer relative to current obligations; accruals booked by firms scoring high on both are the least likely to survive the refinancing calendar.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a targeted sharpening of the archive's best signal: it keeps the accrual leg identical so any change in performance is attributable to adding the cash-coverage dimension to the maturity dimension. A firm with 80% short-term debt but a large cash pile is not liquidity-constrained, and the current conditioner cannot tell it apart from a cash-poor one.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( add( sub( wcap, che ), dlc ), 1 ), dp ), at ), 1 ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( dlc, lt ), neg( ratio( che, lct ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft Asset Build Under Rollover Pressure
input_signals.hypothesis: The reversal-prone element of accruals is the growth of non-cash current assets — receivables and inventory the firm must eventually convert to cash — and it is this asset-side softness, not the working-capital netting of liabilities, that becomes dangerous when debt is maturing.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that Δdlc appears inside the standard accrual numerator, so part of the rollover result could be a mechanical debt-structure effect; this version removes all debt terms from the accrual leg while holding the conditioner fixed, making it a clean attribution test. If the effect survives, the mechanism is genuinely about soft assets meeting short-dated liabilities rather than about debt appearing twice.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), dp ), at ), 1 ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, lt ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft Assets Funded By Maturing Debt
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that expands receivables and inventory while simultaneously increasing its short-dated borrowings has created an explicit maturity mismatch — illiquid soft assets financed by claims that come due within a year — and this specific funding pattern, not accruals or borrowing alone, forecasts distress-driven underperformance.
input_signals.reasoning: The MIN conjunction requires both conditions simultaneously and is not a monotone reweighting of either leg, and the earlier MIN construction with total debt issuance already produced a significant alpha (t = −2.04), so restricting the funding leg to short-maturity debt tests whether maturity is the active ingredient. The accrual leg excludes debt entirely, so the two legs share no mechanical component.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), dp ), at ), 1 ) ), zscore( winsor( ratio( delta( dlc, 1 ), lt ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Three Year Soft Asset Overhang Meets Refinancing
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(TS_SUM(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp), at), 3), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What must be liquidated when debt comes due is the accumulated stock of soft assets, not a single year's flow; three years of uninterrupted, undepreciated working-capital build creates an overhang whose forced unwinding is triggered precisely when short-dated debt and a thin cash buffer force the firm to raise cash from its balance sheet.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the equity-cushion deflator entirely, so it cannot be a microcap scaling artifact, and it changes the accrual leg from a one-year flow to a multi-year stock while holding the liquidity conditioner fixed — a stock-versus-flow lesson the archive has not yet learned on high-coverage data. The earlier cumulative test failed only on 8%-coverage cash-flow lines and with a profitability rather than a liquidity conditioner, so this is a substantively different test rather than a rerun.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ts_sum( ratio( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), dp ), at ), 3 ), 1 ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( dlc, lt ), neg( ratio( che, lct ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Widening Funding Gap
input_signals.expression: RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp)), che), sale), 1), 1))
input_signals.hypothesis: Markets price the level of a liquidity shortfall slowly but may miss its deterioration entirely; a gap that widened over the past year identifies firms whose accrual absorption and refinancing needs are growing faster than their revenue base, which is the state that precedes covenant breach and dilutive issuance.
input_signals.reasoning: Level versus change is a genuine and unresolved lesson in this archive — conditioning on rising leverage worked (alpha −2.8%, t = −3.24) while the level of leverage worked less well — and here it is tested on the construct with the strongest portfolio evidence. A change specification also purges persistent firm characteristics such as capital intensity and industry turnover that the level ratio inevitably carries.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: rank( winsor( delta( ratio( sub( add( dlc, sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), dp ) ), che ), sale ), 1 ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Accruals While Creditors Shorten The Leash
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dltt, lt), 1))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Distress is revealed by the credit supply side: when the long-term share of a firm's liabilities falls, lenders are refusing to term out its debt, and accrual-heavy earnings reported in the same year are precisely the earnings that cannot be validated with cash before the shortened obligations come due.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the static maturity-structure level with a credit-rationing event — the change in the long-term debt share — which is a different economic object: dlc/lt describes how a firm is financed, while a falling dltt/lt says lenders have just changed their willingness to fund it. It therefore reweights an entirely different set of firms than the three archived dlc/lt variants, including levered firms with stable short-term financing that the level conditioner always flags.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( delta( add( sub( wcap, che ), dlc ), 1 ), dp ), at ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( dltt, lt ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt Shortfall Meeting Working Capital Absorption
input_signals.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dlc, ADD(pi, dp)), sale), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The additive gap treats a dollar of maturing debt and a dollar of working-capital absorption as interchangeable, but the distress story says they must coincide: a firm whose cash earnings already fall short of its maturing debt and which is simultaneously pouring cash into receivables and inventory has no way to close the shortfall internally.
input_signals.reasoning: This decomposes the archive's best construct into its two economic pillars and requires both rather than summing them, which is a genuinely different functional form that will flag a different, smaller and more extreme set of firms than the additive gap. It also cleanly separates the two themes across legs — distress in the first, accruals in the second — so a strong result is unambiguously an interaction rather than a re-weighted single-theme effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( dlc, add( pi, dp ) ), sale ), 1 ) ), zscore( winsor( ratio( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), sale ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cash Requirement Without Retained Earnings Fallback
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A cash shortfall is survivable for a firm with a deep stock of accumulated profits and lethal for one financed entirely by external capital, because the latter must return to markets on the market's terms; accumulated retained earnings are the fallback that determines whether a funding gap becomes a distress event.
input_signals.reasoning: Every conditioner tested on the accrual leg has been a flow or maturity variable, and retained earnings — the cumulative internal-capital stock — has never been paired with the funding-gap construct even though it is the classic Altman fragility term. Centering the gap leg keeps the retained-earnings rank as a pure slope modulator, so this asks whether the gap's −5.5% alpha is concentrated in firms with no earned-capital cushion.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( dlc, delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ) ), add( che, add( pi, dp ) ) ), sale ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Full Near Term Claim Stack Versus Cash Earnings
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(lct, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: Trade payables and accrued expenses are claims that come due within the year exactly like maturing debt, so the economically complete near-term claim stack is total current liabilities rather than short-term debt alone, and a firm whose cash earnings and cash balance cannot cover the whole stack plus its working-capital growth is the one that must refinance or liquidate.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has only ever used dlc as the near-term claim, yet generation 3 showed that operating-liability growth carries the *opposite* sign to debt growth, so widening the claim base is a genuine and non-obvious test of whether all near-term claims are equivalent or whether financial claims are uniquely dangerous. If the broader stack performs worse, that pins the mechanism specifically on debt-market refinancing risk rather than on generic liquidity, which sharpens the interpretation of the whole family.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( add( lct, delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ) ), add( che, add( pi, dp ) ) ), sale ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Fragility Score With Accrual Absorption Component
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), at), SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Distress scoring in the Altman-Ohlson tradition uses leverage and earned capital but ignores earnings quality entirely; a firm whose net working-capital absorption is high, whose debt is short-dated, and which has no accumulated retained earnings is fragile in three complementary ways, and accrual quality belongs inside the score as a component rather than as an external conditioner.
input_signals.reasoning: This is built from three raw accounting channels rather than from any archived expression, so it is not a rank-ensemble of previously evaluated signals, and its economic claim — that accrual absorption is a distress *ingredient*, not a distress-conditioned effect — is a structurally different proposition from everything in the archive. Ranking each channel before summing produces the bounded, well-behaved regressor the gap family has lacked, which targets the persistent Fama-MacBeth weakness while keeping three independent sources of return signal in the extreme deciles.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ), at ), sumrank( ratio( dlc, lt ), neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cash Requirement With Weak Debt Coverage
input_signals.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ni, ADD(dlc, dltt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Credit markets do not judge fragility by asset-scaled leverage but by how many years of earnings it would take to retire the debt, so the state that turns an accrual-driven cash requirement into a distress event is a low earnings-to-total-debt multiple, which is exactly the covenant metric lenders actually write.
input_signals.reasoning: Every distress conditioner tested in this archive scales claims by assets, retained earnings or liability composition; none has used the earnings-coverage multiple that determines refinancing terms in practice, and firms with negative earnings automatically land at the fragile extreme with the correct ordering under NEG. Because the conditioner is denominated in debt rather than assets, it reweights asset-light firms with modest book leverage but no earnings — a group every asset-scaled ratio in the archive treats as safe.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( dlc, delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ) ), add( che, add( pi, dp ) ) ), sale ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( ratio( ni, add( dlc, dltt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Absorption Rank Minus Cash Earnings Rank
input_signals.expression: SUB(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(pi, dp), sale), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The accruals-distress interaction can be expressed without any division as the distance between how aggressively a firm is absorbing cash into receivables and inventory and how strongly it is generating cash earnings; firms far up the absorption distribution and far down the cash-generation distribution are the fragile, low-quality-earnings cases.
input_signals.reasoning: This preserves the intensity idea the critic rejected while eliminating the denominator entirely, so there is no near-zero-scale artifact and no non-monotonicity — both legs are separately winsorized, sales-deflated and ranked before differencing. It is also a functional form the archive has never used: a signed rank spread, which is naturally bounded, symmetric and well behaved in a Fama-MacBeth regression, addressing the metric that has plateaued without relying on a monotone rescaling of an existing signal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( rank( winsor( ratio( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), sale ), 1 ) ), rank( winsor( ratio( add( pi, dp ), sale ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Rank Space Funding Identity
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale), SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, sale), NEG(RATIO(ADD(pi, dp), sale))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The cash-requirement identity — working-capital absorption plus maturing debt less cash earnings — is economically meaningful as an ordering of firms on each component, not as a dollar sum, so ranking the three terms separately before combining retains the full economics while removing the dominance of whichever term happens to be numerically largest.
input_signals.reasoning: The dollar-denominated identity yields alphas near −5.5% but slopes capped at −2.3, while the two-component rank spread yields a slope of −2.54 with no alpha, which localizes the problem precisely: rank space fixes the regression but the two-term spread discards the maturing-debt dimension that carries the portfolio payoff. This restores that third component in the same bounded space, which is the one specification the archive has never run and the only construction consistent with both diagnoses.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), sale ), sumrank( ratio( dlc, sale ), neg( ratio( add( pi, dp ), sale ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Free Cash Flow Coverage Of Interest Bearing Debt
input_signals.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(pi, dp), SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1))), ADD(dlc, dltt)), 1)
input_signals.hypothesis: The single number a credit analyst computes is free cash flow to total debt — cash earnings less the working capital they were consumed by, against the borrowings that must eventually be repaid — and equity prices should reward this quantity most where accruals have quietly eroded it.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's coverage constructs all deflate by current or non-long-term liabilities and include the cash stock in the numerator, making them liquidity ratios; this is a pure flow-to-total-debt solvency multiple, a different economic quantity that ranks a cash-poor but strongly converting firm above a cash-rich but absorbing one. It keeps the accrual measure first-order in the numerator — net working-capital absorption is directly subtracted from cash earnings — so earnings quality drives the ratio rather than sitting as a second-order adjustment.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( add( pi, dp ), sub( delta( sub( act, che ), 1 ), delta( sub( sub( lct, dlc ), txp ), 1 ) ) ), add( dlc, dltt ) ), 1 )
